body.text: Calls for control as pigeons damage, defecate and nest on buildings across WA
In short:
Anecdotal reports say pigeons are an increasing problem in regional towns such as Geraldton, Northam and Albany.
While causing hefty damage bills, pigeons also create a human health concern.
What's next?
Business groups, councils and property owners are exploring collaborative control measures.
Increasing numbers of pigeons are defecating and nesting in public buildings across regional Western Australia, racking up damage bills and causing human health concerns.
In Geraldton, 420 kilometres north of Perth, the iconic St Francis Xavier Cathedral, nesting pigeons create an ongoing maintenance and damage bill of up to $15,000 a year.
"The gutters get blocked, the downpipes get blocked and it starts damaging the fabric of the cathedral," said Geraldton diocese director of heritage Robert Cross.
Father Cross said pigeons were causing similar issues in other buildings owned by the Catholic Church in Geraldton.
"They like heights, they like to look down on the rest of us," he said.
Father Cross said any plan of attack needed to include the state's main grain handler, the CBH Group.

"It's really an issue that needs a coordinated approach by those people and places in Geraldton that are either creating a problem, or providing what we just say is pigeon heaven here on Earth," he said.

"Once upon a time you just go out and have a few shots at them and scare them off, but these days we've got all these safety regulations that make it so much more difficult to do something about the problem."
Feed availability
City of Greater Geraldton mayor Jerry Clune agreed Geraldton's pigeon problem was growing due to 'so many feedstocks' being readily available.
"This time of the year of course there's so much grain, not (just) in huge stacks but on the roadside as well so, they're everywhere," he said.
"It becomes a health problem as well, the city are doing their best to control it but if it's not a community effort then those actions will be all in vain."
Mr Clune said the city had previously participated in a joint control program with CBH and the Mid West Ports Authority where pigeons were baited with contraceptive laced grain.

"I think CBH and the port have sort of given up on that, and I think the city will probably move in a similar direction, because there's so many other sources of grain that that is not the solution," he said.
"There's all sorts of ways (to control pigeons), you can anaesthetise them, you can get licensed shooters, you can trap them with a gas type thing.
"It is a community problem, and people who do have properties, then the onus relies with them to take control of what to do with those pigeons.
"Unfortunately around Geraldton we've got a lot of federation style buildings and they've got a lot of ledges and all that and it's perfect for pigeons.
"They just love those sort of buildings and consequently they tell all their mates to come and share the digs with them."
Exterminator prompts police reports
Business owners in Albany, 400km south of Perth, have complained of a spike in pigeon numbers this year with flocks of the bird visible in the CBD and near the port's grain terminal.
Earlier this week, reports of a man with a gun on a building in Albany was actually a pigeon exterminator.
Police issued a public notice after calls were made to emergency services after spotting a man with a firearm on top of a York Street liquor store.
Albany police officer-in-charge Senior Sergeant Carlos Correia said the contractor had not advised authorities of his plans.
"[The contractor] didn't let anybody know and they've been told there is procedures to let people know so we don't scare our community when they see people on a roof with a firearm.
"More often than not they do it at night-time when they can't be seen."
Sergeant Correia thanked the public for being vigilant.
Acid droppings corroding metalwork
Pigeons are causing similar concerns in WA's Avon Valley, 95km north-east of Perth.

Northam Chamber of Commerce chief executive Theresa Lee said she had heard reports of pigeon 'debris' from roof spaces landing on desks in offices, and the chamber was attempting to lead a collaborative control program across Northam.
"We're looking at asset damage, the pigeons (are) affecting corrosion on metal roofing and structural elements due to the acidic nature of their droppings," she said.
"The droppings themselves are highly toxic when they dry, the powder form becomes airborne and can cause up to 28 health conditions in humans if inhaled or ingested."
Ms Lee said the chamber was surveying all businesses to find out where pigeons are nesting across the community in a bid to create a more effective control program.
BirdLife Australia senior adviser Sean Dooley said pigeons were technically rock doves, and were not an ecological threat as they lived near humans.
"They're pretty much street kids really," he said.

"They need buildings and grain or bread or something to feed on, but they are remarkable birds, they've got this reputation as rats with wings and all that sort of stuff but they're incredibly intelligent birds and really adaptable.

"They're one of our oldest domesticated animals and they were initially bred for food but because they have this innate ability to find their way back to their nesting sites, they've been used for communication for centuries."
The ABC has repeatedly requested interviews with the CBH Group.

A 2018 planning document from CBH says pigeons are a "predominant problem in major centres such as ports and major depots" and details CBH's control of pigeons using a narcotic compound in a bait, and shooting.
